items.followUp: Define the anticlockwise moment of a force.

rubric.why: Identifies the quantity as a moment or turning effect acting clockwise.
rubric.description: Names the clockwise turning effect as a moment.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a clockwise moment or turning effect.

rubric.why: A moment describes the turning effect of a force about an axis or pivot.
rubric.description: Relates the moment to a force acting about an axis or pivot.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for referring to a force and an axis or pivot.

modelAnswer: A clockwise moment is the turning effect of a force that tends to rotate an object clockwise about a pivot or axis.

items.followUp: State one condition under which a force does no work.

rubric.why: Work by a force requires the force to cause displacement.
rubric.description: States that the force must cause displacement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking work to displacement caused by the force.

rubric.why: For work to be done, displacement must have a component in the direction of the force.
rubric.description: Relates work to displacement in the direction of the force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the direction condition or giving the work formula.

modelAnswer: A force does work when it causes displacement of an object in the direction of the force.
Work done is the product of the force and the displacement in the direction of the force.

items.followUp: A force of 250 N moves a trolley 12 m in the direction of the force. Find the work done.

rubric.why: The given force and displacement are correctly identified in SI units.
rubric.description: Writes the given data in SI units.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying 400 N and 30 m.

rubric.why: Uses the work formula for force parallel to displacement.
rubric.description: States the formula for work.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for W = Fs.

rubric.why: Shows substitution of the given values into the formula.
rubric.description: Substitutes the values with units.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct substitution.

rubric.why: Gives the correct work and SI unit.
rubric.description: Calculates the work done.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 12,000 J.

modelAnswer: Given: F = 400 N, s = 30 m
Formula: W = Fs
Substitution: W = 400 N × 30 m
Answer: W = 12,000 J

items.followUp: State and prove the law of conservation of momentum for two bodies interacting in the absence of an external force.

rubric.why: The law states that the total momentum of an isolated system remains unchanged.
rubric.description: States the law of conservation of momentum.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for saying that total momentum remains constant when no external force acts.

rubric.why: The proof uses Newton’s third law for the forces between the two bodies.
rubric.description: Applies Newton’s third law.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the interaction forces are equal and opposite.

rubric.why: Relates the forces to the changes in momentum over the same time interval.
rubric.description: Uses force as the rate of change of momentum.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct momentum-change or impulse relation for the two bodies.

rubric.why: The derived result shows that total initial momentum equals total final momentum.
rubric.description: Obtains the conservation equation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct before-and-after momentum equation.

modelAnswer: Consider two bodies of masses m₁ and m₂ with initial velocities u₁ and u₂ and final velocities v₁ and v₂.
During their interaction, the forces on them are F₁₂ and F₂₁ for the same time interval Δt.
By Newton’s third law, F₁₂ = −F₂₁.
Using force as the rate of change of momentum: (m₁v₁ − m₁u₁)/Δt = −(m₂v₂ − m₂u₂)/Δt.
Rearranging gives m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.
Therefore, the total momentum before interaction equals the total momentum after interaction; momentum is conserved when no external force acts.

items.followUp: Define translatory motion and give one example of each of its types.

rubric.why: Translatory motion describes the motion of the whole body without its parts moving in different directions relative to one another.
rubric.description: Defines translatory motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that all parts or points move in the same direction.

rubric.why: Linear motion is translatory motion along a straight path.
rubric.description: Names linear motion and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct linear-motion example, such as a car moving along a straight road.

rubric.why: Circular motion is one type of translatory motion in the textbook classification.
rubric.description: Names circular motion and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct circular-motion example, such as a body moving in a circular path.

rubric.why: Random motion is motion along an irregular, unpredictable path.
rubric.description: Names random motion and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct random-motion example, such as gas molecules moving randomly.

modelAnswer: Translatory motion is motion in which all parts of a body move the same distance in the same direction in the same time interval.
Linear motion is motion along a straight line; for example, a car moving along a straight road.
Circular motion is motion along a circular path; for example, a body moving in a circle.
Random motion is motion along an irregular path; for example, gas molecules moving randomly.

items.followUp: Define a couple and calculate its torque if each force is 15 N and the perpendicular distance between their lines of action is 0.4 m.

rubric.why: A couple consists of two forces equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and parallel.
rubric.description: Identifies the two forces that form a couple.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the equal, opposite, parallel forces.

rubric.why: The forces must act along different lines of action to produce a turning effect.
rubric.description: States that the forces have separated lines of action.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting the separation or perpendicular distance between their lines of action.

rubric.why: The torque of a couple is the product of either force and the perpendicular distance between the forces.
rubric.description: Gives the torque formula for a couple.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula and meaning of the distance.

rubric.why: A couple produces rotation, and its torque measures that turning effect.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of a couple.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the couple causes rotation or a turning effect.

modelAnswer: A couple is a pair of equal, opposite and parallel forces whose lines of action are separated.
The torque due to a couple is the product of either force and the perpendicular distance between the lines of action of the forces.
Torque of a couple: τ = Fd.
This torque produces a turning effect or rotation.

items.followUp: How many significant figures are there in the measurement 0.00450 m?

rubric.why: Significant figures include the reliably known digits of a measurement.
rubric.description: Identifies the reliable or accurately known digits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for referring to reliable, certain, or accurately known digits.

rubric.why: The first uncertain or doubtful digit is included in the significant figures.
rubric.description: Includes the first uncertain digit in the definition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning the first uncertain or doubtful digit.

modelAnswer: The significant figures of a measurement are all its accurately known digits together with the first uncertain (doubtful) digit.

items.followUp: Why are very small time intervals important when studying rapid physical processes?

rubric.why: Very small intervals are needed to time events that happen rapidly.
rubric.description: Explains that small intervals are needed for rapid events.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking small time intervals to fast or rapid processes.

rubric.why: Measuring these intervals helps determine how long a rapid event takes or how it changes with time.
rubric.description: States what measuring small intervals helps determine.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that measurement reveals the duration or time behaviour of a rapid event.

modelAnswer: We need to measure extremely small time intervals to study events that occur very rapidly.
Measuring them lets us determine the duration and changes of these fast processes.
